position: Additional Areas for Reform (Cyber Threat Intelligence)
proposal: The Mandate recommends that the intelligence community adopt an obligation-to-share policy, with write-to-release products that provide new technical indicators and targeting information relevant to cyber defense to the public or targeted entities within 48 hours of collection, with agency heads able to withhold for operational or counterintelligence reasons but reporting the number and justification of exceptions to Congress. status_summary: No IC obligation-to-share policy with a 48-hour release rule, exception reporting to Congress, or real-time access auditing was found. The nearest federal action concerns the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015, which governs sharing by private companies with the government: it lapsed on 2025-09-30, was extended in a late-2025 stopgap through 2026-01-30, then through 2026-09-30 in a consolidated appropriations act enacted in early February 2026, and a stopgap funding bill passed by the House on 2026-09-01 moves its expiration to 2026-12-11. The National Cyber Director said on 2026-05-07 that the administration wants long-term reauthorization and is developing faster two-way sharing. These steps are parallel and do not set the Mandate's IC release rule.

timeline.event: The original ten-year term of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 ended; a temporary extension enacted in late 2025 ran through 2026-01-30.
A law-firm post reported that a consolidated appropriations act enacted in early February 2026 (H.R. 7148) had moved the 2015 law's sunset to 2026-09-30.

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross said the administration is pushing for long-term reauthorization of the 2015 law and is developing faster, more actionable two-way information sharing with the private sector.
The House approved a stopgap funding bill that moves the law's expiration from 2026-09-30 to 2026-12-11; the report said the President was expected to sign it.
A CRS update lists the law's provisions as expiring 2026-12-11 after enactment of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027.

title: Adopt an obligation-to-share policy with 48-hour release of cyber threat intelligence
uncertainties: The 2015 law is about voluntary sharing by companies with the government and is not an IC release policy, so it is related background only. The CRS update says the provisions were extended to 2026-12-11 upon enactment of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, without a public law number or date; the Nextgov article of 2026-09-01 said the stopgap was not yet signed, so the CRS statement is the basis for treating it as enacted. The February 2026 act's public law number and exact date were not found. A search for an ODNI or NSA write-to-release or 48-hour policy returned nothing new; the Senate intelligence committee's FY2027 bill (S. 4615) lists a section making hostile foreign cyber actors a national intelligence priority but none on release of indicators, by title. Internal IC sharing policies may not be public. Checked systematically on 2026-10-18: Federal Register API searches (three term variants) found no IC release policy or 48-hour rule; the Unified Agenda listing was unreachable and the CISA-filtered queries failed; one congress.gov and govinfo search matched only 112th to 114th Congress bills; the ODNI newsroom showed nothing on cyber indicator release (CISA and NSA pages could not be fetched); and one news search found only reports of faster sharing of unclassified indicators. Executive Order 14306 (signed 2025-06-06) and Executive Order 14390 (signed 2026-03-06), read in review, set no IC release deadline, exception reporting or access auditing; the first removed an earlier directive to establish procedures to immediately share threat information. Internal IC sharing policies may not be public, and enacted 119th Congress laws were not read for such provisions.
